summary: This section explains how directors are first chosen and later elected for a Producer Company. The founders can name the first board in their founding documents, but proper elections must happen soon after registration. It also sets rules for how long directors can serve and lets the board add expert or additional directors under certain limits.
points: Founders who sign the memorandum and articles can name a first Board of Directors of at least five members to run the company until elections take place.
Elections for directors must happen within ninety days of the company registration, except for certain inter-State co-operative societies which get up to three hundred and sixty-five days.
A director must hold office for a period between one year and five years as specified in the articles.
Retiring directors are allowed to be re-appointed if the rules permit.
Members must elect or appoint directors at the annual general meeting, except for the first board.
The board can add expert or additional directors up to one-fifth of the total number of directors, subject to the rules in the articles.
example: A group of farmers decided to start a producer business named Green Valley Producer Company Limited. The founders who signed the articles named seven initial directors to manage the company affairs right away. Within ninety days of registering the company, Green Valley held its proper elections as required. During the annual general meeting, the members formally elected their directors to serve for a term of two years. Later, the board wanted extra guidance and used their power to add an expert director, ensuring the total number of added and expert directors did not exceed one-fifth of the whole board.
